paragraphs.title: The Prophet Awaits an Answer and the Righteous Live by Faith

easy.explanation: He says, “I will stand upon my watch.”
easy.q: Where does the prophet stand while waiting for God's answer?

easy.explanation: The LORD says, “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables.”
easy.q: What does the LORD command the prophet to do with the vision?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “the just shall live by his faith.”

answers: So that the reader might run with it
So that the nations could not understand it
So that the waiting would end immediately
medium.explanation: It was to be plain “that he may run that readeth it.”
medium.q: Why was the vision to be written plainly upon tables?

answers: It will come at the appointed time
medium.explanation: The vision is “for an appointed time” and “will surely come.”
medium.q: What does the LORD promise about the vision?

medium.explanation: The verse contrasts the proud, lifted-up soul with the just who live by faith.
medium.q: What is meant by the soul that is “lifted up”?

challenge.explanation: He waits to see “what I shall answer when I am reproved.”
challenge.q: What is the prophet prepared to do after receiving God's answer?

answers: Between the rich and the poor
Between the proud and the just
Between a city and a village
challenge.explanation: The verse contrasts the soul that is not upright with the just who live by faith.
challenge.q: What central contrast appears in verse 4?

challenge.explanation: The command is, “though it tarry, wait for it.”
challenge.q: What should a person do if the vision seems to tarry?

paragraphs.title: The Arrogant Conqueror and the Beginning of His Downfall

easy.q: How is the man who gathers nations described?

easy.explanation: His desire is enlarged “as hell,” and he is “as death, and cannot be satisfied.”
easy.q: What is the conqueror compared to in his insatiable desire?

answers: Take up a parable and taunting proverb against him
easy.explanation: They will “take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb.”
easy.q: What will the nations eventually do to the conqueror?

answers: Because he spoiled nations and shed blood
medium.explanation: He spoiled many nations and acted through bloodshed and violence.
medium.q: Why will the nations rise against the conqueror?

medium.explanation: The phrase “ladeth himself with thick clay” pictures a heavy burden laid upon him.
medium.q: What does “thick clay” represent in the passage?

answers: The conqueror gathers nations, they rise against him, and they spoil him
The conqueror is spoiled, and then he gathers nations
The nations build his power, and he gives it away
medium.explanation: He first gathers and oppresses nations, but they later rise and take his possessions.
medium.q: What sequence is described in these verses?

answers: That he is satisfied with little
That he is never satisfied and always wants more
challenge.explanation: Like death, he cannot be satisfied and continually gathers more people.
challenge.q: What does the comparison of the conqueror to death emphasize?

answers: They will attack and trouble him
challenge.explanation: Those who bite and vex him are the nations rising against him.
challenge.q: What does it mean that others shall “bite” him?

challenge.explanation: His pride, greed, and violent ambition bring judgment upon him.
challenge.q: What moral quality leads to the conqueror's downfall?

paragraphs.title: Stolen Wealth and the City Built Through Wrongdoing

easy.explanation: He covets “an evil covetousness to his house.”
easy.q: What does the ruler seek in order to secure his house?

easy.explanation: He builds a town “with blood” and establishes a city “by iniquity.”
easy.q: What is the city built with?

answers: The knowledge of the glory of the LORD
easy.explanation: The earth shall be filled with “the knowledge of the glory of the LORD.”

answers: They were built through violence and wrongdoing
medium.explanation: His house and city are founded on evil gain, blood, and iniquity.
medium.q: Why will the ruler's wealth and city fail to give him true security?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “the beam out of the timber shall answer it.”
medium.q: What does the beam from the timber do in the passage?

answers: The building itself testifies against the wrongdoing used to make it
The building was made without workers
medium.explanation: The crying stone and answering beam picture the injustice crying out from the structure.
medium.q: What relationship exists between the stones, the beam, and the city's construction?

answers: Human labor based on injustice will be vain, while God's glory will spread
The nations will succeed more than the LORD
challenge.explanation: The people's labor is described as vanity, while the knowledge of God's glory will fill the earth.
challenge.q: What contrast is shown between the nations' labor and the filling of the earth with God's glory?

answers: The injustice of the building will be exposed
The city will be built quickly
challenge.explanation: The image shows that the wrongdoing connected with the building cannot remain hidden.
challenge.q: What can be understood from the words, “the stone shall cry out of the wall”?

answers: Human effort without righteousness cannot succeed against God's judgment
The nations have conquered the LORD
The phrase describes the city's builders
challenge.explanation: The passage attributes the final outcome to the LORD and calls unjust labor vanity.
challenge.q: What does “of the LORD of hosts” emphasize concerning the people's labor?

answers: He makes them drunk in order to shame them
easy.explanation: He gives his neighbor drink and makes him drunken so that he may look on his nakedness.
easy.q: What does the ruler do to others with drink?

answers: The cup of the LORD's right hand
easy.explanation: The cup of the LORD's right hand shall be turned unto him.
easy.q: What will the ruler eventually drink?

answers: Violence against the land, animals, and people
easy.explanation: The passage mentions Lebanon, beasts, blood, the land, the city, and all who dwell therein.
easy.q: What violence will return upon the ruler?

medium.explanation: The one who shamed others will himself receive shame and punishment.
medium.q: What principle connects the ruler's actions with his punishment?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes the ruler's humiliating treatment of those he makes drunk.
medium.q: What does “look on their nakedness” mean in this context?

answers: He changes from one who shames others to one who receives shame
He changes from poor to wealthy
He changes from fugitive to deliverer
medium.explanation: His shameful actions return upon him, and he is filled with shame instead of glory.
medium.q: How does the ruler's condition change by the end of the passage?

answers: To show the wide extent of the violence he caused
To explain how the city was built
challenge.explanation: The passage shows that his violence affected people, animals, cities, and the land.
challenge.q: Why are animals and the land mentioned along with people?

answers: Judgment and punishment coming upon him
challenge.explanation: The cup represents the judgment that will be turned upon the ruler.
challenge.q: What does the cup of the LORD's right hand symbolize here?

answers: The ruler who was filled with glory will be filled with shame
challenge.explanation: The passage says, “Thou art filled with shame for glory.”
challenge.q: What connection is made between glory and shame?

paragraphs.title: Mute Idols Versus the Lord in His Holy Temple

easy.explanation: The passage describes images made by their makers and covered with gold and silver.
easy.q: What kind of objects are described as graven or molten images?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “there is no breath at all in the midst of it.”
easy.q: What is lacking in the dumb idol?

answers: In the center of the city
easy.explanation: The verse declares, “the LORD is in his holy temple.”
easy.q: Where is the LORD according to the final verse?

answers: Because the idol has no life or power
Because the idol is too large
Because the idol is made of gold
medium.explanation: The idol is made by a human craftsman but cannot speak, teach, or act.
medium.q: Why does the prophet ask, “What profiteth the graven image”?

medium.explanation: In the KJV, “dumb” means silent or unable to speak.
medium.q: What does the word “dumb” mean when describing the idols?

answers: The idols are silent and lifeless, but the LORD is in His holy temple
The idols are alive, but the LORD is silent
There is no contrast between them
medium.explanation: The idols have no breath, while the LORD is present in His holy temple.
medium.q: What contrast is made between the idols and the LORD?

answers: All should be silent in reverence before the LORD
All should flee from the earth
challenge.explanation: The command calls the whole earth to acknowledge the LORD with reverence.
challenge.q: What does the command “Let all the earth keep silence before him” mean?

answers: They trust in a man-made object with no breath or power
They trust in something living and strong
They obey the command to be silent
challenge.explanation: The idol is made by human hands and has no breath in it.
challenge.q: What criticism is made of those who trust in an idol?

answers: By calling all the earth to be silent before the LORD in His temple
By promising wealth to the nations
challenge.explanation: The final verse turns attention from powerless idols and rulers to the LORD in His holy temple.
challenge.q: How does chapter 2 conclude the contrast between human power and the LORD?
